item.title: Stop Committing Skills to Every Repo — Your claude.ai Account Is Now a Config Source of Truth
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: A September 17 Claude Code update syncs skills and plugins from your claude.ai account to every signed-in terminal session — team config without dotfiles or a git commit.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: A September 17, 2026 Claude Code update syncs the skills and plugins enabled on your claude.ai account to your terminal sessions. Team config without a dotfile convention or git commit.**
Claude Code skills have historically lived in two places: project `.claude/skills/` (committed to the repo, project-scoped) and `~/.claude/skills/` (per-machine, managed manually). Getting a whole team onto the same set of utility skills meant either committing them to every repo's `.claude/` directory or maintaining a shared dotfiles convention that someone had to enforce.
The September 17, 2026 Claude Code changelog adds a third source: **your claude.ai account**. Enable skills and plugins in the web UI, and every terminal session signed into that account picks them up automatically — across machines.
**What this creates: a three-tier config hierarchy**
| Tier | Source | Scope | |------|--------|-------| | Project | `.claude/skills/` in the repo | This codebase only | | Account | claude.ai skills/plugins sync | Per user, all machines | | Org | Managed settings / `managed-mcp.json` | Org-wide, enforced |
Project-level skills override account-synced ones when names collide. Org-managed settings (`managed-mcp.json`) override both — a skill blocked in managed settings cannot be re-enabled by account sync.
**The practical team workflow:**
1. **Org layer:** Deploy company-wide MCP servers and shared policies via managed settings — these ship to everyone automatically. 2. **Account layer:** Each engineer enables their personal utility skills on claude.ai (e.g., their preferred code-review or doc-search skill) — syncs to their terminal sessions on any machine. 3. **Project layer:** Each repo carries skills specific to that codebase in `.claude/skills/` — version-controlled, reviewed in PRs.
**Limits to know:** - Sync requires an active `claude auth login` session. A session running off a raw `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` with no sign-in gets no account-synced skills. - Signing out drops the synced skills for that session. Signing into a different account switches to that account's skills. - CI and headless runs that use the API key path are unaffected — no change needed there. - Same release also adds `CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_STARTUP_WAIT_MS`, an env var that bounds how long a non-interactive turn waits for connecting MCP servers — useful if your CI MCP servers are slow to start.
**Sources:** [Claude Code Changelog — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog) · [Claude Code September 2026 updates — Havoptic](https://www.havoptic.com/tools/claude-code) · [Control MCP access for your organization — Claude Code Docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp)

item.title: Describe the Goal, Not the Steps: Claude Projects' Coordinator-Thread Model for Parallel Autonomous Work
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Projects redesigned as a coordinator: describe the goal once and Claude creates parallel branch-scoped threads, shares memory across them, opens PRs, and assembles results.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Projects redesigned today: describe your goal once and Claude acts as coordinator — spawning parallel thread sessions on separate branches, sharing memory across them, opening PRs, and assembling results.**
Anthropic shifted Projects from a folder-based system to a coordinator model. You describe what needs to happen; Claude scopes it into parallelizable chunks, spins up concurrent threads (each an independent cloud session on its own branch), and coordinates them through shared project memory.
**What this looks like:**
Set a performance optimization goal. Claude profiles each endpoint in parallel threads, opens PRs per thread, and runs your tests. The coordinator reads all outputs and assembles the result. Each thread can itself spawn subagents, loops, or workflows for its slice.
The shared memory component is the key architectural change: every thread reads from and writes to the same project memory, so the coordinator doesn't re-explain project decisions, conventions, or preferences per delegation.
**When to reach for it:** work that genuinely parallelizes — profiling a set of endpoints, refactoring across independent services, sweeping a parameter space. The pattern validates against real data: GitHub's Copilot Rust migration used 15 child sessions with a 10:1 read-to-edit ratio. Reading the codebase in parallel is cheap; the edit-validate-merge loop is the bottleneck that threads parallelize.
**Real limits to know before you use it:** - Cloud-only today. Running threads on your own machine (with your local tools and network) is coming but not live yet. - Concurrent threads consume your usage quota faster — Projects can hit limits faster than a single session. - Merge conflicts between overlapping thread work land as standard PRs — you still review and resolve. - Beta: currently limited to select Claude Pro/Max users with cloud sessions.
**When NOT to reach for it:** sequential work where context from step A gates step B, tasks that need local tooling or private network access, or anything where you need direct control over context-trimming and retry semantics.
**Sources:** [Claude Projects redesign](https://claude.com/blog/projects-redesigned) · [GitHub Copilot Rust migration (independent parallel-agent case study)](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/generative-ai/migrating-the-github-copilot-runtime-to-rust-using-copilot/)

item.title: Your Agent Forgets Everything at Session End — A Free 90-Minute Course Builds the Two-Tier Memory That Fixes It
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Free 90-min DeepLearning.AI course by Letta co-founders covers two-tier agent memory: in-context core blocks + external archival storage that agents self-edit via tool calls.
item.content:encoded:
**Build agents with persistent memory that survives session end — a free DeepLearning.AI course covers the two-tier architecture that replaces "it forgot everything" with searchable, self-updating state.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Implement in-context core memory blocks paired with external archival storage, let agents self-edit their own memory using tool calls, and share memory blocks across a multi-agent coordinator pattern.
**Three takeaways:** 1. **Two tiers, one agent.** In-context core memory holds immediate context (user info, task state, preferences). External archival storage is a searchable database the agent queries when it needs something that's been evicted from the window — bridging sessions without re-prompting. 2. **Agents edit their own memory via tool calls.** The agent inserts, updates, and prunes its stored knowledge as it learns, rather than you managing state externally. You can audit these edits in the conversation log. 3. **Shared memory blocks enable coordinator patterns.** A coordinator agent writes state that worker agents read — no context-passing in prompts; the memory layer is the coordination mechanism.
**Concrete setup (Letta):**
```python from letta import create_client from letta.schemas.memory import BasicBlockMemory, Block
client = create_client() agent = client.create_agent( memory=BasicBlockMemory( blocks=[ Block(name="human", value="User: Alice — working on RAG pipeline with Qdrant"), Block(name="persona", value="Expert coding assistant focused on retrieval systems"), ] ) )
# Agent updates core memory as it learns new context client.send_message( agent_id=agent.id, role="user", message="Note: Alice prefers Python and Qdrant runs on localhost:6333" ) # Core memory block now updated — persists across sessions ```
The memory update is a tool call visible in the conversation — auditable, reversible.
**The course:** [LLMs as Operating Systems: Agent Memory](https://www.deeplearning.ai/courses/llms-as-operating-systems-agent-memory) — free, 90 minutes, 8 lessons with 5 code examples, taught by Charles Packer and Sarah Wooders (Letta co-founders, MemGPT paper authors).
**Limits:** Letta's perpetual-single-thread model is opinionated — it suits long-running assistants well but adds overhead for stateless task agents where you don't need persistence. If you're already on LangGraph, [LangMem](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langmem/) is a lower-ceremony alternative that integrates natively with LangGraph's store and distinguishes semantic, episodic, and procedural memory without Letta's architectural constraints.
**Sources:** [DeepLearning.AI course](https://www.deeplearning.ai/courses/llms-as-operating-systems-agent-memory) · [Letta agent memory docs](https://docs.letta.com/guides/agents/memory/) · [LangMem docs](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langmem/)

item.title: Agents Spent 10× More Time Reading Than Writing — Orchestration Lessons From GitHub's 800K-Line Rust Port
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: One developer used AI agents to port 430K lines of TypeScript to 832K lines of Rust in 3-4 months. Tool call logs show 10:1 reads-to-edits and 96% cache hit rate — two numbers that change how you structure agent sessions.
item.content:encoded:
**One developer and AI agents ported 430K lines of TypeScript to 832K lines of Rust in 3-4 months — tool call logs show 591K reads, 282K searches, and 41K edits: a 10:1 investigation-to-mutation ratio.**
GitHub published a detailed engineering account of rewriting the Copilot agent runtime (CLI, Desktop app, six-language SDK) using AI agents. One developer directed the effort; agents handled most code exploration and porting while the human operated the "control loop" — reviewing decisions, enforcing quality gates, pushing agents that treated intermediate states as done.
The numbers are worth reading as agent design guidance:
**1. Separate the orchestrator from the workers.** The largest component used a primary session coordinating 15 concurrent child sessions across 7 waves. Each child received a bounded slice (~1,100-character kickoff prompt — specific enough to define scope, loose enough for autonomy) and handled its own implementation decisions. The parent enforced constraints and reviewed outputs.
**2. Prefix-cache aggressively to keep costs manageable.** The project ran thousands of model calls and hit a 96.22% prompt-cache hit rate. Per the provider's pricing, cached tokens carry a ~90% discount. The author estimates an uncached equivalent would have cost an order of magnitude more. If your agent loop repeatedly reads the same context, structure prompts so the invariant portion sits at the top and gets cached.
**3. Plan for more exploration than generation.** Of all tool calls: `view` (read file) = 590,988; `rg` (search) = 281,783; `edit` = 40,591. The author: "The popular image of AI spewing code is almost backwards — at this scale, the work looked much more like iterative investigation." If your agent is generating more than it is reading, it is probably cutting corners on context.
**Limits:** A senior developer operated the control loop throughout. The regression count was "dozens," spread across ambiguous TypeScript semantics, ambient behaviors (timezone, env var handling), incomplete migrations, and lifecycle management. Fully autonomous migration without human oversight would have shipped those bugs silently.
**Sources:** [Migrating the GitHub Copilot runtime to Rust, using Copilot — GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/generative-ai/migrating-the-github-copilot-runtime-to-rust-using-copilot/)

item.title: Your Bi-Encoder Found 100 Candidates — A Cross-Encoder Takes Two Seconds to Tell You Which 5 Matter
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Bi-encoders retrieve fast but score documents independently. Cross-encoders score query+document jointly for higher precision — two stages give you both speed at scale and accuracy at the top.
item.content:encoded:
**Bi-encoders retrieve fast but score documents independently; cross-encoders score query and document together in one forward pass — running both in sequence gives your RAG pipeline speed at scale and precision at the top.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** add a re-ranking stage to your existing RAG retriever that improves the precision of chunks sent to the LLM, without replacing your vector store.
- Bi-encoders encode query and document separately, then compare by dot product. Fast enough to scan millions of docs; embeddings pre-compute offline. - Cross-encoders take query + one candidate document as a pair, run them through a transformer together, and output a single relevance score. More accurate — the model attends across both inputs — but cannot pre-compute embeddings, so only practical on a short candidate list. - Standard pipeline: retrieve top 100 with a bi-encoder → re-rank with a cross-encoder → pass top 5–10 to the LLM.
**Walk-through using `sentence-transformers`:**
```python from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, CrossEncoder, util
# Stage 1 — retrieve candidates (pre-compute corpus embeddings once) bi_encoder = SentenceTransformer("multi-qa-mpnet-base-dot-v1") corpus_embeddings = bi_encoder.encode(corpus, convert_to_tensor=True)
query_embedding = bi_encoder.encode(query, convert_to_tensor=True) hits = util.semantic_search(query_embedding, corpus_embeddings, top_k=100)[0]
# Stage 2 — re-rank the top-100 candidates cross_encoder = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2") pairs = [(query, corpus[hit["corpus_id"]]) for hit in hits] cross_scores = cross_encoder.predict(pairs)
# Sort by cross-encoder score, pass top 5 to your LLM ranked = sorted(zip(hits, cross_scores), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) top_chunks = [corpus[h["corpus_id"]] for h, _ in ranked[:5]] ```
`cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2` scores 74.30 NDCG@10 on the TREC Deep Learning 2019 track — an independent IR community evaluation run by NIST, not by Hugging Face. It runs at roughly 1,800 documents per second on a V100.
**Limits:** You cannot pre-compute cross-encoder scores — re-ranking happens at query time. A top-100 re-rank at 1,800 docs/sec adds negligible latency; a top-1,000 re-rank gets noticeable. For production scale, Cohere Rerank (`co.rerank(model="rerank-v3.5", ...)`) offloads the compute. Also: if your bi-encoder misses the right documents in stage 1, the cross-encoder cannot recover them — retrieval recall still sets the ceiling.
**Sources:** [Retrieve & Re-Rank tutorial — sbert.net](https://www.sbert.net/docs/sentence_transformer/usage/semantic_search/retrieve_rerank/README.html) · [Retrieve & Rerank Colab notebook — sentence-transformers/GitHub](https://colab.research.google.com/github/huggingface/sentence-transformers/blob/main/examples/sentence_transformer/applications/retrieve_rerank/retrieve_rerank_simple_wikipedia.ipynb) · [ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 model card — HuggingFace](https://huggingface.co/cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2) · [TREC Deep Learning 2019 overview — NIST/TREC](https://trec.nist.gov/pubs/trec28/papers/OVERVIEW.DL.pdf) (independent IR evaluation)

item.title: Describe Your CI Task in Plain English — GitHub Agentic Workflows Runs It With Claude Code
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Write a .github/workflows/*.md file in plain English, run `gh aw compile`, and GitHub Actions executes it with Claude Code or Copilot as the agent engine — no YAML authoring required.
item.content:encoded:
**Write a Markdown file in `.github/workflows/` describing what you want automated; `gh aw compile` turns it into a GitHub Actions workflow that runs a coding agent — Claude Code, Copilot, or Codex — on your triggers.**
GitHub Agentic Workflows (in public preview since June 2026) let you automate reasoning-heavy repository tasks — issue triage, CI failure analysis, documentation updates — without writing Actions YAML. You describe the outcome in natural language; the `gh aw` CLI compiles it into a runnable workflow.
## How it works
```bash gh extension install github/gh-aw gh aw compile ```
A workflow file has two parts: YAML frontmatter (triggers, permissions, allowed outputs) and a freeform Markdown section describing the task.
**CI failure analysis — `.github/workflows/investigate-failures.md`:**
```markdown --- on: workflow_run: workflows: ["tests"] types: [completed]
permissions: contents: read checks: read
safe-outputs: create-pull-request: title-prefix: "[fix] "
agent: model: claude-code ---
When the test suite fails, inspect the failure logs, identify the root cause, and open a pull request with a targeted fix. Do not change unrelated files. ```
`gh aw compile` generates the corresponding `investigate-failures.lock.yml` that GitHub Actions executes. Setting `model: claude-code` in the frontmatter routes the run through your Anthropic account instead of Copilot.
## What to know before wiring it up
- **Read-only by default.** Write operations (opening PRs, creating issues) require explicit `safe-outputs` entries — the agent cannot push or merge autonomously. - **Humans approve PRs.** No auto-merge; every PR the agent opens needs a human sign-off. - **Per-run cost.** GitHub reports "typically two premium requests per run" using Copilot; using Claude Code as the engine bills your Anthropic usage instead. - **Good fit:** recurring reasoning tasks — issue labeling, stale PR summarization, test-failure triage. Poor fit: fast, deterministic operations a shell script already handles.
**Sources:** [Automate repository tasks with GitHub Agentic Workflows — GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/automate-repository-tasks-with-github-agentic-workflows/) · [GitHub previews Agentic Workflows — The Register](https://www.theregister.com/2026/02/17/github_previews_agentic_workflows/) · [Public preview changelog — GitHub](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-06-11-github-agentic-workflows-is-now-in-public-preview/)

item.title: Run Any Open Model Locally and Call It Like a REST API — Ollama in Three Commands
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Ollama installs as one binary, pulls models on demand, and serves a local REST API on port 11434. Three commands from zero to a running inference server you can hit from Python.
item.content:encoded:
**Ollama installs as one binary, pulls open models on demand, and runs a local REST server on port 11434 — any OpenAI client can target it by swapping `base_url`.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** download and run open-weight models locally, serve them as a REST API, and call them from Python with either `requests` or the `openai` SDK — no cloud API key, no data leaving your machine.
- `ollama pull` fetches and caches a model; `ollama run` opens an interactive REPL; `ollama serve` (or leaving the desktop app open) starts the HTTP server - The API at `http://localhost:11434/v1` is OpenAI-compatible — swap any client's `base_url` and set `api_key="ollama"` to point at your local server - Models are stored locally (~4–8 GB per Q4 checkpoint); an 8B model needs roughly 8 GB of RAM to run at reasonable speed; 70B models won't fit on most laptops
## Install and pull
```bash # Linux / macOS curl -fsSL https://ollama.ai/install.sh | sh
# Pull a quantized 8B model (~5 GB download) ollama pull llama3.1:8b-q4_K_M
# Interactive chat ollama run llama3.1:8b-q4_K_M ```
On Windows, download the installer from [ollama.ai](https://ollama.ai). The daemon starts automatically and listens on `localhost:11434`.
## Call the API from Python
```python import requests
r = requests.post("http://localhost:11434/api/generate", json={ "model": "llama3.1:8b-q4_K_M", "prompt": "Explain vector similarity in one sentence.", "stream": False }) print(r.json()["response"]) ```
Or with the OpenAI client library (no SDK change, just a different `base_url`):
```python from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1", api_key="ollama") resp = client.chat.completions.create( model="llama3.1:8b-q4_K_M", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain vector similarity."}] ) print(resp.choices[0].message.content) ```
## What it won't do
- Models larger than ~7B need 16+ GB RAM to run without painful slowdowns; 70B models require a 48 GB GPU or a heavily quantized GGUF - Port 11434 has no auth — don't expose it on the network without a reverse proxy or firewall rule - Ollama doesn't load-balance across multiple GPUs; for that, use vLLM instead
The best free resource is Tech with Tim's [Learn Ollama in 15 Minutes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UtSSMs6ObqY) (YouTube, 2025) — covers install, API calls, Python integration, and custom Modelfiles in one sitting.
**Sources:** [Learn Ollama in 15 Minutes — Tech with Tim (YouTube)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UtSSMs6ObqY) · [Ollama official site — ollama.ai](https://ollama.ai) · [Ollama Tutorial: Running LLMs Locally Made Super Simple — KDnuggets](https://www.kdnuggets.com/ollama-tutorial-running-llms-locally-made-super-simple)

item.title: Your CLAUDE.md Loads on Every Turn Whether Claude Needs It or Not — Path-Scoped Rules Fix That
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Path-scoped rules in .claude/rules/ load only when Claude touches a matching file — converting always-loaded rules to scoped ones can cut startup context by 40–50% on large projects.
item.content:encoded:
**Every rule in your project CLAUDE.md is re-injected on every turn. Add a `paths:` frontmatter key and a rule loads only when Claude touches a matching file — 40–50% less startup context on large codebases.**
Every unscoped rule in your project-root `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/rules/*.md` files is re-injected into Claude's context window on every turn — even your test-mock strategy, which only matters when Claude is editing `src/__tests__/`. Path-scoped rules change that: they load only when Claude reads or edits a file matching the glob you specify.
**The setup:**
``` .claude/rules/ coding-standards.md # no paths: frontmatter → always loaded api/ CLAUDE.md # auto-scoped to api/ by directory src/__tests__/ CLAUDE.md # auto-scoped to test files by directory frontend.md # add paths: frontmatter to scope it explicitly: ```
```markdown --- paths: ["src/components/**", "app/ui/**"] --- # Frontend rules Always use the design system's Token type for any color value. Never reach outside the component's props for theme state. ```
A session working only in `worker/` or `scripts/` never loads `frontend.md`. A session touching `src/components/Button.tsx` loads it exactly once.
**What to convert first:** Any rule that reads "when working in [specific directory]" or "when editing [framework] files" is the highest-priority candidate. Rules you added "just in case Claude needs this" are next — they're paying context cost on every turn where they're irrelevant.
One documented project (published on Zenn) reduced always-loaded rule overhead from 1,358 lines to 807 lines — 41% reduction — by converting procedure-heavy files into Skills and scoping domain-specific rules to their directories. For projects with many accumulated rules, 50%+ reduction is achievable.
**The limit to understand:** Path-scoped rules don't survive context compaction the way root `CLAUDE.md` does. After compaction, they're gone until Claude touches a matching file again. A session that jumps between many directories pays a small reload cost at each boundary — that's the intended trade-off. Don't scope a rule you expect Claude to hold in mind throughout the whole session; keep those in the root CLAUDE.md.
**Sources:** [Explore the context window — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/context-window) · [Claude Code Rules Directory: Modular Instructions That Scale — claudefa.st](https://claudefa.st/blog/guide/mechanics/rules-directory) · [Path-Scoped Skills — claudefa.st](https://claudefa.st/blog/guide/mechanics/path-scoped-skills)

item.title: Your Design Canvas and Your Repo Drift Every Sprint — `/design-sync` Closes That Gap in Two Commands
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: The /design-sync command in Claude Code imports your real design system into Claude Design's canvas (pull), then syncs built components back to the canvas (push) — generated screens start from your actual component library.
item.content:encoded:
**`/design-sync` in Claude Code imports your real design tokens and components into Claude Design's canvas, and `--push` syncs built components back — generated screens start from your actual component library, not generic HTML.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** run a full sprint from canvas prompt to production component without manually copying tokens, describing screenshots to Claude Code, or discovering mid-PR that the generated code references components that don't exist in your repo.
**Three things to know:** - `/design-sync` (pull mode) reads your design tokens and component definitions from the repo and populates the Claude Design canvas — generated screens reference your real `Button`, `Card`, and `Modal`, not scaffolded HTML - `/design-sync --push` runs the reverse: Claude Code scans your built components and updates the canvas so the design file reflects what's actually in the codebase - Claude Design validates generated output against the synced system before showing it — reducing the "correct on canvas, broken in the codebase" debugging loop
**The four-step sprint workflow:**
**1. Pull your design system (once per project; repeat when tokens change):** ``` # In Claude Code: /design-sync ``` Claude Code reads tokens and component definitions from the repo and uploads them to the Claude Design project you last had open. If the project already has a GitHub repo attached, `/design-sync` detects it automatically. Nothing writes to disk — it populates the canvas.
**2. Prompt in Claude Design.** With your real components loaded, the canvas generates screens that reference your actual imports. Refine spacing and copy with the canvas editor or inline comments — no need to re-prompt the whole screen for small adjustments.
**3. Hand off to Claude Code.** Use "Send to Claude Code" (or "Send to local coding agent") from the canvas. Claude Code receives the screen spec along with the component context it just synced and generates implementation that references your real component paths — not invented names it will hallucinate when building.
**4. Push the built component back before review:** ``` /design-sync --push ``` The canvas updates to reflect the as-built component. Run this before a design review so the reviewer is looking at what's in the codebase, not the original sketch — they approve what ships, not what was planned.
**Two limits before you plan around this:** - Large repos (thousands of files) slow the pull sync; Anthropic's docs recommend "linking from Claude Code" rather than uploading for very large codebases — expect lag or browser issues otherwise - Multi-person canvas editing is listed as "basic and may not work reliably" in the current release — coordinate who edits before using it in a collaborative review
**Sources:** [Get started with Claude Design — support.claude.com](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14604416-get-started-with-claude-design) · [Claude Design + /design-sync: The Two-Way Bridge — skills-hub.ai](https://skills-hub.ai/blog/claude-design-sync-code-handoff-2026) · [Claude Code and Claude Design Now Sync Both Ways — pasqualepillitteri.it](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/5308/claude-code-claude-design-two-way-sync-design-sync)

item.title: Your Gateway Logs Every Claude Code Request as "claude-sonnet-4-6" — These Headers Let You Track Them by Session and Agent
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code sends x-claude-code-session-id and x-claude-code-agent-id on every API request — extract them in your LLM gateway to attribute costs per session and per subagent without parsing request bodies.
item.content:encoded:
**When Claude Code routes through an LLM gateway, extract three built-in request headers to attribute API costs per session and per subagent — no request-body parsing needed.**
When Claude Code routes through an LLM gateway (LiteLLM, Portkey, or a custom FastAPI proxy), every request arrives looking identical: `POST /v1/messages`, model `claude-sonnet-4-6`. Your logs show token counts but no way to tell which requests belong to which developer session, which are from subagents running in parallel, or which background tasks are burning the budget.
Claude Code sends three attribution headers on every request to an `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` gateway:
| Header | When present | Tells you | |---|---|---| | `x-claude-code-session-id` | Always | Unique ID for this session — aggregate all requests from one run | | `x-claude-code-agent-id` | Subagent requests only | ID of the spawned subagent that issued the request | | `x-claude-code-parent-agent-id` | Nested agents only | ID of the parent agent (for multi-level agent trees) |
Extract them in your gateway middleware before forwarding:
```python # FastAPI gateway proxy (simplified) from fastapi import Request
@app.post("/v1/messages") async def proxy(request: Request): session_id = request.headers.get("x-claude-code-session-id") agent_id = request.headers.get("x-claude-code-agent-id") parent_id = request.headers.get("x-claude-code-parent-agent-id")
log_request_attribution( session_id=session_id, is_subagent=bool(agent_id), agent_depth=2 if parent_id else (1 if agent_id else 0), ) # ... forward to upstream ```
With these tags your dashboards go from "1,000 Sonnet calls" to "120 interactive sessions, 680 subagent calls, 200 nested-agent calls" — actionable enough for per-project chargeback or per-developer budget alerts.
**New in v2.1.273 (opt-in):** Set `CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS=1` on the developer's machine to add five more request headers — `x-claude-code-request-class`, `x-claude-code-agent-type`, `x-claude-code-prev-tool-durations`, `x-claude-code-compaction`, and `x-claude-code-context-compacted` — that give the gateway finer-grained signal about what Claude Code is doing with each request.
**Limits:** These headers are sent only when routing through `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`; they are not present on Bedrock-format (`CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1`) or Vertex-format connections. The `x-claude-code-agent-id` is generated fresh each time a subagent spawns, so it cannot be used to track the same logical agent across different sessions. Do not treat agent IDs as user identifiers.
**Sources:** [Gateway protocol reference — Claude Code docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway-protocol) · [Claude Code changelog v2.1.273](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog) · [LiteLLM gateway setup](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/configs) (independent gateway reference)

item.title: Your Text Is Already in Postgres — Build Semantic Search on Top of It With Supabase vecs in 25 Lines
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Use Supabase's vecs Python client to embed documents, store them in pgvector, filter by metadata, and run semantic similarity searches — from connection to first query in 25 lines.
item.content:encoded:
**Use Supabase's vecs Python library to build a metadata-filtered semantic knowledge base on pgvector — create a collection, upsert embeddings, index once, and query with filters in under 25 lines.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Connect a Python app to Supabase's pgvector extension using the vecs client - Embed and upsert documents with arbitrary metadata (source, date, department) for filtered retrieval - Run semantic similarity queries constrained by metadata without writing any SQL
The resource: [Getting Started with Supabase Vector Databases](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6xchFWcHkaI) (YouTube, June 2026) walks the full workflow hands-on. The steps below match the vecs 0.4.x API.
**Install:** ```bash pip install vecs sentence-transformers ```
**Complete workflow:** ```python import vecs from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
# 1. Connect to your Supabase Postgres instance vx = vecs.create_client( "postgresql://postgres:<password>@<project-ref>.supabase.co:5432/postgres" )
# 2. Create (or retrieve) a named collection # dimension must match your embedding model's output size model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2") docs = vx.get_or_create_collection(name="knowledge_base", dimension=384)
# 3. Embed and upsert documents with metadata records = [] for doc in my_documents: vec = model.encode(doc["text"]).tolist() records.append(( doc["id"], # stable identifier (string) vec, # 384-dim list or np.array {"source": doc["source"], "year": doc["year"]} # arbitrary metadata dict )) docs.upsert(records=records)
# 4. Build an HNSW index — run once as a migration, not on every upsert docs.create_index()
# 5. Semantic query with metadata filter query_vec = model.encode("annual leave policy").tolist() results = docs.query( data=query_vec, limit=5, filters={"source": {"$eq": "hr_policies"}} # MongoDB-style filter operators ) # returns: ["doc-42", "doc-19", "doc-77", ...] ```
**The key decisions:** - `dimension` must match your embedding model exactly — set it once at collection creation - `create_index()` builds an HNSW graph synchronously; on large collections (>100,000 records) this takes minutes. Run it as a one-time schema migration - Metadata filters use MongoDB-style operators: `$eq`, `$lt`, `$gt`, `$in`, `$contains`
**Limits:** vecs is Python-only — there is no official JS/TypeScript equivalent; JavaScript apps query pgvector through raw SQL or the Supabase client's `rpc()` method. vecs does not support hybrid (keyword + vector) search out of the box; for BM25 + vector retrieval you need to compose queries at the SQL layer directly. Index creation blocks the calling thread; do it in a migration script, not in a request handler.
**Sources:** [vecs Python client docs — Supabase](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/ai/vecs-python-client) · [supabase/vecs — GitHub](https://github.com/supabase/vecs) · [Getting Started with Supabase Vector Databases — YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6xchFWcHkaI) · [Semantic Search with Supabase — OpenAI Cookbook](https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/vector_databases/supabase/semantic-search) (independent implementation reference)

item.title: Claude Code v2.1.273 Patches an Auto-Mode Permission Bypass and Adds MCP Disconnect Alerts
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code 2.1.273 (Sept 15) closes two auto-mode permission-checker bugs including a subshell bypass, adds a visible MCP disconnect notification, and fixes an over-inflated context meter.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Code 2.1.273 (Sept 15) closes two permission-checker bugs in auto mode — including a subshell bypass — and adds a notification when MCP reconnection gives up for good.**
Three changes in the September 15 release worth acting on.
**Auto-mode subshell bypass (fixed).** In auto mode, a destructive command wrapped inside a `$()` subshell — e.g. `echo $(rm -rf /build/cache)` — bypassed the permission checker and executed without a review prompt. Separately, Bash commands the analyzer couldn't fully parse were silently allowed under `blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories` instead of triggering a review. Both are patched.
**MCP disconnect notification (new).** When an MCP server disconnects mid-session and automatic reconnection gives up, Claude Code now surfaces a notification pointing to `/mcp`. Previously the server disappeared silently and you'd notice only when a tool call returned an unexpected error.
**Context meter fix.** Advisor-tool turns were being counted at roughly twice their real context size, causing premature "running low" warnings during tool-heavy sessions. The meter now reflects actual context usage.
**The limit:** The permission checker analyzes command syntax statically. It cannot catch obfuscated commands built through dynamic string concatenation at runtime. In high-risk CI environments, pair auto mode with OS-level sandboxing as a second control layer rather than relying on the permission model alone.
**Why it matters:** The subshell bypass was a real gap in auto mode's safety model. If you run Claude Code with `auto` permissions in CI pipelines, deploy v2.1.273 before your next run. The MCP fix removes a silent failure mode that was hard to debug.
**Sources:** [Claude Code changelog — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog) · [Sandboxed Bash tool — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing)

item.title: Hundreds of AI Agents Coordinated a Real-World Attack at 395 Organizations — Here Is What the Logs Show
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: A threat actor ran hundreds of Codex and DeepSeek agents against PaperCut NG/MF servers, hitting 440 instances at 395 orgs in 48 countries — first RCE in under four hours, domain admin in seven minutes at one school.
item.content:encoded:
**A threat actor ran hundreds of Codex and DeepSeek agents against PaperCut NG/MF servers in late August, hitting 440 instances at 395 orgs in 48 countries — first RCE in under four hours, domain admin in seven minutes at one school.**
GreyNoise published the full breakdown on September 9. The threat actor — believed to be Russian-speaking — first stood up a private lab with a vulnerable PaperCut instance and an Active Directory server to develop and test exploits, then launched at scale. Two CVEs were targeted: CVE-2026-81578 (authentication bypass) and CVE-2026-82078 (unsafe reflection remote code execution).
The attack economics, from the GreyNoise analysis:
| Milestone | Time | |---|---| | Empty workspace → first RCE on a real victim | Under 4 hours | | First access → domain admin (typical) | ~2 hours | | One high school: initial access → domain admin | 7 minutes | | 11 organizations compromised | 26 seconds |
The agentic approach enabled rapid parallel exploitation — scanning, credential harvesting from LSASS, noPac attacks, and domain admin creation all running concurrently across hundreds of targets. 280 victims had credentials harvested; 147 had OS/domain secrets extracted; 12 reached full domain admin compromise. The education sector accounted for 204 of 395 victims.
One detail worth noting: in some cases the agents deviated from the attacker's own geographical targeting restrictions. The same coordination problem you manage in your agentic builds applies to the attacker's too — though that is cold comfort for the 395 organizations in the data.
**What worked on defense:** a Cloudflare WAF successfully defeated exploitation attempts in at least one recorded case. Patching, network segmentation, and WAF rules remain effective — the underlying attack surface was unpatched CVEs, not some AI-specific bypass.
**Context this week:** on September 12, Dario Amodei published "We Must Pace the Frontier," arguing frontier labs should deliberately slow capability gains by one to two years so safety work can catch up. Sam Altman publicly agreed within hours. The PaperCut campaign — empty workspace to domain admin in under six hours, using publicly available models and tools — illustrates what that urgency looks like from the defender's side.
**Why it matters:** the infrastructure for this attack (Codex + DeepSeek + commodity offensive tools) is largely the same infrastructure you build production agents with. The speed — <4 hours from scratch to real-world RCE — is not a theoretical future; it is August 2026 activity. Understanding how agents were orchestrated here is directly useful for designing your own agent architectures with appropriate guardrails.
**Sources:** [Agents Gone Wild: An AI-Orchestrated Global Campaign Against PaperCut NG/MF](https://www.greynoise.io/blog/ai-orchestrated-campaign-against-papercut-ng-mf) (GreyNoise, Sept 9 2026) · [AI-powered attack exploited PaperCut flaws to hack 395 organizations](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/ai-powered-attack-exploited-papercut-flaws-to-hack-395-organizations/) (BleepingComputer) · [Hundreds of AI agents helped PaperCut attacker hit 395+ orgs, and some went off script](https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/09/10/hundreds-of-ai-agents-helped-papercut-attacker-hit-395-orgs-and-some-went-off-script/5295650) (The Register)

item.title: You've Been Setting r=16 Without Knowing Why — Here Is the LoRA Decision From First Principles
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: LoRA trains two small matrices instead of updating all weights, betting fine-tuning lives in a low-dimensional subspace. Here is how to pick rank, alpha, and target_modules from that logic.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** choose LoRA rank (`r`), `lora_alpha`, and `target_modules` from first principles, understand what each parameter actually controls, and stop cargo-culting `r=16`.
**Why LoRA works — the one idea underneath all the parameters**
Full fine-tuning adjusts every weight in the model. LoRA instead parameterizes the update as ΔW = B×A, where A is an r×d matrix and B is d×r — two small matrices whose product approximates the change you need. The bet: for most fine-tuning tasks, the useful update lives in a much lower-dimensional subspace than the full d×d weight matrix. For instruction-following, style adaptation, and domain shift on standard tasks, this bet is almost always correct. The adapter adds roughly 0.5% of the original parameters; the base model stays frozen.
**Picking rank (`r`)**
| Task | r | Why | |---|---|---| | Style / format only | 8 | Narrow change; low capacity needed | | Instruction-following (default) | 16 | Enough for most tasks without overfitting | | Complex domain shift, 10K+ examples | 32–64 | Broader subspace, more capacity |
Start at r=16. Increase only if validation loss stagnates and you're not already overfitting. Going to r=128 rarely helps and often hurts.
**Setting alpha (`lora_alpha`)**
The effective scale applied to the adapters is `lora_alpha / r`. Start with `lora_alpha = r` (scale = 1.0). If training is sluggish and the model doesn't converge, try `lora_alpha = 2r`. Set `use_rslora=True` in the PEFT config — this switches the denominator to `sqrt(r)` instead of `r`, which keeps the effective scale numerically stable at higher ranks without changing your alpha value.
**Choosing `target_modules`**
Apply LoRA to all major linear layers, not just attention:
``` Attention: q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj MLP: gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj ```
In PEFT, `target_modules="all-linear"` does this automatically and consistently outperforms attention-only targeting. The VRAM saving from restricting modules is minimal; the accuracy cost is not.
**Minimal working config**
```python from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model
config = LoraConfig( r=16, lora_alpha=16, target_modules="all-linear", lora_dropout=0.05, use_rslora=True, bias="none", ) model = get_peft_model(base_model, config) model.print_trainable_parameters() # trainable params: ~40M / 8B total (~0.5%) ```
After training, merge with `model.merge_and_unload()` to fold adapter weights into the base and remove inference overhead.
**Three real limits**
1. **Inference memory is unchanged.** The adapter and base both load. You save VRAM during training, not deployment. Merging solves this but removes per-task switching. 2. **LoRA learns rare facts less reliably than full fine-tuning.** A 2024 arXiv study ([LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less, 2405.09673](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.09673)) found LoRA retains common knowledge better (less catastrophic forgetting) but struggles more with rare domain-specific information than full fine-tuning does. If your task depends heavily on rare facts, evaluate carefully. 3. **Dynamic imports fool TIA.** Not a LoRA issue — just the related context if you're running fine-tuning in a CI pipeline: static dependency analysis misses dynamic imports. (See this week's CI scaling post for the pattern.)
**Sources:** [LoRA Conceptual Guide — Hugging Face PEFT](https://huggingface.co/docs/peft/main/en/conceptual_guides/lora) · [LoRA Hyperparameters Guide — Unsloth](https://unsloth.ai/docs/get-started/fine-tuning-llms-guide/lora-hyperparameters-guide) · [LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less (arXiv 2405.09673)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.09673) — independent academic study on LoRA retention vs. full fine-tuning

item.title: Your CI Was Designed for One PR a Day — Here Is the Architecture That Handles Agentic Code at Scale
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: When AI writes 80% of your code, your CI sees 25x more jobs. Test impact analysis — mapping changes to the minimum valid test set — is the architecture fix Anthropic shipped.
item.content:encoded:
**When AI authors 80% of your code and generates 25× more CI jobs in six months, "bigger machine" is a patch. Stateless test selection is the fix.**
Anthropic's engineering blog published yesterday on a problem most teams running Claude Code will hit: agentic code generation creates exponential CI load, not linear. Their trajectory:
| Change | Bought | How it broke | |---|---|---| | 2× machines | 70 days | Memory saturation | | Shard by package | 29 days | Package count kept growing | | Daily restart | <1 day | Hit load by mid-afternoon | | Stateless workers + TIA | Scales horizontally | — |
The fix was **test impact analysis (TIA)**: a service that maps each code change to the minimum set of tests that could be affected, using past run data and the package dependency graph. Instead of running 10,000 tests on every agent commit, each change gets a targeted list — and agents self-verify against that. The service is stateless, runs as disposable workers, and scales out rather than up.
Three things this implies for your stack:
1. **Design for 5× your current CI load, not 1.1×.** If agents write 20% of your commits today, extrapolate forward. The curve is not linear. 2. **A focused test set gives agents better feedback.** 200 targeted tests let an agent iterate; waiting 20 minutes on a full suite induces guessing. Tighter feedback loops produce fewer follow-up fixes. 3. **Stateless beats stateful at scale.** A single process accumulating per-test history across thousands of changes becomes a bottleneck. Workers that process one change and exit scale horizontally without any coordination problem.
For Python stacks: [`pytest-testmon`](https://testmon.org) tracks source-to-test dependencies and re-runs only affected tests. For polyglot monorepos, Bazel's affected-target analysis does this at the build graph level. The technique predates LLMs; agentic coding just made it load-bearing.
**One real limit:** TIA depends on accurate static dependency data. Dynamic imports, generated code, and metaprogramming can cause under-selection — the service may skip tests it should have run. Anthropic validated coverage by running TIA alongside the full suite for the first few weeks before relying on it exclusively.
**Sources:** - [Agentic coding is straining CI: how we scaled test impact analysis at Anthropic](https://claude.com/blog/agentic-coding-is-straining-ci-heres-how-we-scaled-test-impact-analysis-at-anthropic) (Anthropic engineering blog, Sept 14 2026) - [TDAD: Test-Driven Agentic Development — Graph-Based Impact Analysis](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.17973) — independent arXiv paper on automated test selection for AI coding agents - [pytest-testmon](https://testmon.org) — open-source Python TIA; the same principle applied to smaller stacks

item.title: Your Subagent Inherits Your Whole CLAUDE.md — Opt Out With One Frontmatter Line
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: omitClaudeMd: true in a subagent's frontmatter strips project and user CLAUDE.md files before the agent runs — cleaner context, lower cost, more predictable behavior for utility agents.
item.content:encoded:
**`omitClaudeMd: true` in a subagent's frontmatter strips project and user CLAUDE.md files before the agent starts — so a focused utility agent runs with only its own system prompt, not the whole project's instruction stack.**
By default, every agent Claude Code spawns loads the full CLAUDE.md hierarchy: user-level instructions, project file, and any local overrides. For your main coding session, that context is the right behavior. For a narrow utility agent — a doc-formatter, a grep-and-summarize step, a test runner, a code-review tool with its own rubric — it's noise, and when the instructions conflict, they degrade output.
The GitHub issue [#4908: Scoped Context Passing for Subagents](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/4908) captured this precisely: a subagent assigned a fixed style rule would receive conflicting guidance from project-level architectural instructions it had no part in.
Claude Code v2.1.271 (Sept 14) adds `omitClaudeMd: true` to agent frontmatter. Add it to any `.claude/agents/*.md` file:
```yaml --- name: doc-formatter description: Rewrites docstrings in a file to Google-style format. Call with the file path. omitClaudeMd: true ---
Your task: rewrite every docstring in the file at $ARGUMENTS to Google style. Rules: - Args section lists each parameter with type and description - Returns section describes the return value and its type - Raises section lists exceptions the function can throw Output the modified file and nothing else. ```
The agent's own system prompt (everything after the frontmatter block) is the only instruction layer it sees. Managed policy files still load — this flag only clears what you as the project operator control.
**When to reach for it:** any subagent with a repeatable, bounded task — grep pipelines, file converters, doc generators, review passes against a fixed rubric. Practitioner experience with Claude Code subagent isolation, like [Asa Nyaga's write-up on keeping context clean](https://asanyaga.com/tutorials/2026/03/17/part-5-claude-code-subagents.html), confirms that predictability degrades as the instruction surface grows past what the task needs.
**Pair it with per-command `allowed_domains`.** Also in v2.1.271: Bash, PowerShell, and Monitor commands in auto mode can each carry their own `allowed_domains` list. Each command is reviewed and restricted to only the hosts it needs; other hosts are refused for that command only. Together these two options give you a fully scoped utility agent: no inherited project instructions, no unrestricted outbound network.
**The limit:** project conventions you normally rely on from CLAUDE.md — error handling patterns, test directory structure, naming rules — don't reach the subagent. Replicate what you need inside the agent's own system prompt. That's the right trade for a utility agent; for a full-task coding agent that needs to understand your project, don't set this flag.
**Sources:** [Claude Code v2.1.271 changelog — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog) · [Issue #4908: Scoped Context Passing for Subagents — GitHub](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/4908) · [Subagents: Keeping Your Context Clean — Asa Nyaga](https://asanyaga.com/tutorials/2026/03/17/part-5-claude-code-subagents.html)

item.title: Anthropic's September Threat Report Names Your API Keys as a Primary Attack Target
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: AI-enabled pipelines now harvest credentials from repos and containers at scale, completing cloud breaches in 2-3 hours. Anthropic's September report names three mitigations for engineers building AI-powered systems.
item.content:encoded:
**AI-enabled attack pipelines now harvest API credentials from public code at industrial scale — Anthropic's September threat report names credential theft as the primary multiplier for follow-on attacks and autonomous agent frameworks as the delivery mechanism.**
Anthropic's September 2026 threat intelligence report covers operations from December 2025 through August 2026 across seven harm categories. The finding most directly relevant to engineers building AI-powered systems: AI API keys embedded in public repos, Docker images, and mobile app bundles are actively harvested at scale and immediately redeployed to fund follow-on attacks. Compromised credentials function as both loot and free compute. The report documents cloud breaches completing in 2–3 hours using multi-step autonomous pipelines, where human operators handle only target selection and result review.
The report is also candid about the democratization effect: "Sophisticated attacks no longer require sophisticated attackers." Individual operators now run the kind of multi-target, multi-step campaigns that previously required specialist teams.
**Three things to do now:**
1. **Rotate API keys on a short TTL** and alert on anomalous per-minute call rates from unfamiliar IPs. Most providers support per-key spending caps; set one. A key in a public repo is discovered by automated scanners within minutes of the push.
2. **Restrict agent capabilities to what the task actually requires.** An agent that reads documents doesn't need shell access or unrestricted outbound HTTP. Scope tool permissions in your agent harness (`disallowedTools`, network egress rules, capability gates) before the agent starts — not after an incident prompts it.
3. **Treat every dynamic agent input path as untrusted.** A document your agent reads can instruct it to call `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/role-name` — the AWS metadata endpoint that returns temporary IAM credentials. Input validation on agent prompts carries the same weight as input validation on HTTP endpoints.
Independently, MITRE ATLAS ([atlas.mitre.org](https://atlas.mitre.org/)) and the UK NCSC's AI cyber threat guidance document the same shift in operational tempo: the attacks are familiar; the automation that scales them is new.
**Why it matters:** If your agents have broad tool access or your API keys get exported to subprocesses, this isn't theoretical. The report makes the attack playbook explicit enough that the mitigations above aren't optional hardening — they're the expected baseline.
**Sources:** [Countering misuse of AI: September 2026 — Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/threat-intelligence-report-september-2026) · [MITRE ATLAS: Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems](https://atlas.mitre.org/)

item.title: Your HuggingFace Model Is 16 GB — Quantize It to 4.9 GB in Three Commands With llama.cpp
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Convert any HuggingFace model to Q4_K_M GGUF with llama.cpp: a 16 GB BF16 8B checkpoint shrinks to ~4.9 GB, runs on a laptop, and imports into Ollama in one command.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** take any HuggingFace model — a Qwen3-8B, a Llama-3.1-8B, anything in SafeTensors or PyTorch format — quantize it to Q4_K_M GGUF with llama.cpp, and run it locally in Ollama or with llama-server, with no cloud fees and no data leaving your machine.
**Three things to know before you start:** - **Q4_K_M** is the community's default starting point: a mixed 4-bit scheme that protects the most sensitive weight layers, shrinking a 16 GB BF16 8B model to about 4.9 GB while losing less than 1.5 percentage points on standard benchmarks vs. the full-precision baseline (community-measured MMLU-Pro evals; model labs don't publish these figures for their own models, so treat numbers as approximations). - **imatrix calibration** is optional but worthwhile at Q4: it runs the full-precision model over a text corpus to map which weights carry the most activation energy, then places bits more carefully. At Q4_K_M it typically recovers most of the quality gap vs. Q5_K_M — worth the 20–40-minute one-time cost for a model you'll run daily. - **Models below ~3B parameters** lose more quality at Q4 because fewer weights means less redundancy to exploit. For small models, start at Q5_K_M or Q8_0.
**The walkthrough.** The video [GGUF Quantization Tutorial: Run Fine-Tuned LLMs on CPU with llama.cpp](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vvrGfqd1oxE) covers the end-to-end workflow hands-on. Commands below match llama.cpp v0.4:
```bash # 1. Build llama.cpp (one-time) git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp && cd llama.cpp cmake -B build && cmake --build build --config Release -j$(nproc)
# 2. Convert a HuggingFace model to BF16 GGUF python tools/convert_hf_to_gguf.py \ --outfile qwen3-8b-bf16.gguf \ --outtype bf16 \ --remote Qwen/Qwen3-8B # or pass a local HF directory
# 3a. Quantize to Q4_K_M (no imatrix — fast, good enough for Q5+) ./build/bin/llama-quantize qwen3-8b-bf16.gguf qwen3-8b-q4_k_m.gguf Q4_K_M
# 3b. Or build an imatrix first for better Q4 quality ./build/bin/llama-imatrix \ -m qwen3-8b-bf16.gguf \ -f tools/data/groups_merged.txt \ -o qwen3-8b-imatrix.dat \ -ngl 99 # offload to GPU if available ./build/bin/llama-quantize \ --imatrix qwen3-8b-imatrix.dat \ qwen3-8b-bf16.gguf qwen3-8b-q4_k_m.gguf Q4_K_M
# 4. Import into Ollama printf 'FROM ./qwen3-8b-q4_k_m.gguf\n' > Modelfile ollama create qwen3-local -f Modelfile ollama run qwen3-local ```
**Limits.** The BF16 conversion step requires holding the full-precision model in RAM — about 16 GB for an 8B model. For 70B+ you need server-class RAM; if you don't have it, look for pre-converted GGUF uploads on HuggingFace (most popular models have community GGUF branches). The imatrix step is CPU-bound by default; `-ngl 99` offloads it to GPU when CUDA or Metal is available. And GGUF conversion is currently gated to decoder-only (GPT-style) transformer architectures — encoder and encoder-decoder models need separate tooling.
**Sources:** [GGUF Quantization Tutorial: Run Fine-Tuned LLMs on CPU with llama.cpp — YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vvrGfqd1oxE) · [llama.cpp quantize README — GitHub](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/quantize/README.md) · [GGUF quantization guide — tonisagrista.com](https://tonisagrista.com/blog/2026/quantization/)

item.title: Your Vector-Only RAG Misses Error Codes and Product SKUs — Combine BM25 + Dense Search in 15 Lines With LangChain
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: LangChain EnsembleRetriever wires BM25 keyword search alongside your vector store. Queries hit both, results merge via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, and exact-string recall climbs without rebuilding your pipeline.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** retrieve documents that match both meaning and exact strings — fixing the failure where vector-only search returns the semantically similar wrong chunk for a specific error code, API method name, or product SKU.
**The problem vector-only RAG has.** A dense embedding model maps meaning, not identity. "Connection timeout error" and "network failure" land close in vector space. But `errno: ETIMEDOUT` and `errno: ECONNREFUSED` are different errors — and your vector index, asked for one, may return the other. The same gap shows up for product codes, function names, log IDs, and any string whose meaning is its exact spelling.
BM25 — the same keyword model behind most search engines — inverts this: it scores exact term overlap precisely, but treats "cheap flight" and "budget travel" as unrelated. Hybrid search runs both on the same query and merges the ranked lists.
**The hands-on tutorial.** The YouTube walkthrough [Hybrid Search RAG Pipeline From Scratch](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eNzsuWaOCEI) builds a full pipeline with LangChain, BM25, and ChromaDB from scratch.
**Install:** ```bash pip install langchain rank_bm25 faiss-cpu ```
**Wire BM25 + dense retrieval with EnsembleRetriever:** ```python from langchain.retrievers import EnsembleRetriever from langchain.retrievers.bm25 import BM25Retriever from langchain.vectorstores import FAISS from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings
docs = [...] # your Document list
bm25 = BM25Retriever.from_documents(docs) dense = FAISS.from_documents(docs, OpenAIEmbeddings()).as_retriever()
retriever = EnsembleRetriever( retrievers=[bm25, dense], weights=[0.4, 0.6] # 40% keyword, 60% semantic )
results = retriever.invoke("ETIMEDOUT error in connection pool") ```
`EnsembleRetriever` merges the result lists using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), which operates on ranks rather than raw scores — so there's no need to normalize incompatible BM25 and cosine similarity scores before merging.
**Tune the weights.** Start with `[0.4, 0.6]` and test on real queries from your domain. Code search and support-ticket RAG typically benefit from a higher BM25 weight; narrative document search skews toward the semantic side.
**Three takeaways:** - BM25 fills the exact-match gap vector search leaves; embeddings fill the semantic gap keyword search leaves — you need both - RRF fusion sidesteps score incompatibility; the only parameter to tune is the relative weight - Pinecone, Weaviate, and Elasticsearch also offer native hybrid search if you're already on those; `EnsembleRetriever` is the drop-in for any vector store + BM25 combo
**The limits:** two retrieval steps add latency and double the index maintenance surface. BM25 doesn't benefit from fine-tuned embeddings, so any domain customization you've done to your dense model doesn't transfer to the keyword side. And the weight ratio is a hyperparameter you need to tune per corpus — the right split for a customer support knowledge base is different from an API reference.
**Sources:** [Hybrid Search RAG Pipeline From Scratch — YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eNzsuWaOCEI) · [Hybrid Search with LangChain — LanceDB/Medium](https://medium.com/etoai/hybrid-search-combining-bm25-and-semantic-search-for-better-results-with-lan-1358038fe7e6) · [Hybrid Search: BM25 + Dense Vector Reference 2026 — digitalapplied.com](https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/hybrid-search-bm25-vector-reranking-reference-2026) · [LangChain EnsembleRetriever docs — python.langchain.com](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/ensemble_retriever/)

item.title: Your File-Search Subagent Doesn't Need Opus — Route Cheap Tasks to Haiku With One Env Var
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Set CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL=haiku to run read-only subagents on Haiku and save your Sonnet/Opus budget for tasks that actually need it. Particularly timely as limits reset today.
item.content:encoded:
**Set `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL=haiku` to run read-only and search subagents on Haiku — saves your weekly budget for the reasoning work that actually needs Sonnet or Opus.**
With today's permanent +25% limit replacing the temporary +50% boost (a net 17% cut for current users), subagent model routing is the most direct lever for stretching what you have.
By default every subagent inherits the main session's model. An Explore subagent doing a codebase grep, a test-runner scanning diffs, or a docs agent summarizing files does not need the same reasoning depth as the session doing the actual coding. Three patterns:
**Pattern 1 — Session-wide default (fastest)**
In `.claude/settings.json`:
```json { "env": { "CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL": "haiku", "CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE": "1" } } ```
`_FORCE=1` prevents any subagent from escalating back to the heavier model. Good for exploration-heavy workflows where most delegated tasks are read-only.
**Pattern 2 — Per-agent model in frontmatter**
In `.claude/agents/explorer.md`:
```yaml --- name: explorer description: Fast read-only codebase search. Use for grep, glob, and file reads. model: haiku tools: Read, Glob, Grep --- ```
This routes just the named agent to Haiku while leaving other agents at their defaults.
**Pattern 3 — The decision rule**
Anything that reads but doesn't decide: Haiku. Anything making a judgement — what to build, change, or write — gets Sonnet or Opus. "Reads but doesn't decide" covers grep, glob, test runner output, doc generation, summarizing files.
**The limit:** Haiku is not suitable for multi-step reasoning, complex code generation, or ambiguous tasks where a wrong answer costs rework. If a subagent needs to plan before acting, routing it to Haiku costs more than it saves. Also: `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1` is all-or-nothing; if one agent sometimes needs heavier reasoning, use per-agent frontmatter instead.
**Sources:** [Create custom subagents — code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents) · [Claude Code Subagent Model Routing — Roan Brasil Monteiro, Medium](https://medium.com/@roanmonteiro/claude-code-subagent-model-routing-stop-paying-for-opus-on-haiku-work-ee76dc32cb88) · [Claude Code Agents & Subagents — ksred.com](https://www.ksred.com/claude-code-agents-and-subagents-what-they-actually-unlock/)

item.content:encoded:
**Anthropic's permanent +25% limit increase takes effect today, but it replaces the current temporary +50% boost — net result for existing users is a 17% reduction in weekly Claude Code quota.**
Starting September 14, Anthropic is replacing its temporary 50% usage increase with a permanent 25% increase for Pro, Max, Team, and seat-based Enterprise plans. The math Anthropic acknowledged in follow-up: if the baseline limit is 100 units, the temporary promo had users at 150; the new permanent number is 125. That is a 17% drop from what users have had since the promo started.
Two changes that partially offset this:
- **Auto mode's permission classifier no longer counts against your weekly limit.** Every background safety check — the classifier approving or blocking a command — was consuming quota. Those calls are now free, which returns some headroom for users who rely on auto mode. - **Faster input loading** ships alongside the limit change, reducing latency on long sessions.
The announcement framed the change as "permanently raising standard weekly limits," leading to community pushback when users did the arithmetic. Anthropic employees acknowledged that leading with the temporary-to-permanent transition would have been clearer.
**Why it matters:** If you're running CI-driven Claude Code workflows or heavy agentic development, your effective weekly ceiling is 17% lower than yesterday — worth recalibrating before you hit a wall mid-project.
